Virginia property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • Local real estate assessors must assess at 100 percent fair market value in localities with annual assessments. (Va. Code 58.1-3201; source)
  • Local board of equalization hears complaints and may increase or decrease assessments; assessor's valuation is presumed correct. (Va. Code 58.1-3379; source)
  • On appeal to the board, taxpayer must show by a preponderance of the evidence that property is valued above fair market value or not uniformly assessed. (Va. Code 58.1-3379; source)
  • Market sales through December 31 before the assessment's effective date may be considered if submitted by the locality's application deadline. (Va. Code 58.1-3379; source)
  • Application to the commissioner of the revenue for correction: within three years from the last day of the tax year, or one year from assessment date, whichever is later; real estate corrections limited to errors by the commissioner or factual errors in reassessment. (Va. Code 58.1-3980; source)
  • Relief may be sought in circuit court within three years of the last day of the tax year, or one year from assessment or final determination, whichever is later. (Va. Code 58.1-3984; source)
  • In circuit court proceedings, the taxpayer burden of proof applies except in proceedings seeking relief from real property taxes. (Va. Code 58.1-3984; source)
  • Real estate with taxes delinquent on December 31 after the second anniversary of the due date may be sold (first anniversary for condemned, nuisance, derelict, or blighted property). (Va. Code 58.1-3965; source)
  • Property assessed at $100,000 or less may be sold on court finding of taxes delinquent after first anniversary. (Va. Code 58.1-3965; source)

Virginia offers property tax relief for qualifying homeowners, and official sources explain the rules.

What the official sources say

  • Localities may by ordinance exempt or defer real estate taxes for owner-occupied sole dwellings of persons at least 65 or, if the ordinance provides, permanently and totally disabled. (Va. Code 58.1-3210; source)
  • Real property of a veteran rated 100 percent service-connected, permanent and total disabled, occupied as principal residence, is exempt from real property tax (tax years from 2011). (Va. Code 58.1-3219.5; source)
  • Surviving spouse of an eligible veteran qualifies so long as the spouse does not remarry. (Va. Code 58.1-3219.5; source)
  • Creditor-process homestead exemption: $5,000 ($10,000 if age 65+), plus up to $50,000 in value for principal residence of householder or dependents, plus $500 per dependent. (Va. Code 34-4; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Virginia evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law.

What the official sources say

  • Henrico General District Court: effective July 1, 2026, filing an unlawful detainer requires a 14-day Pay or Quit Notice under 55.1-1245 and certification of the Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities (55.1-1204). (Henrico GDC Unlawful Detainers; source)
  • Nonpayment: landlord may terminate if tenant fails to pay within 14 days after written notice (version shown on this page). (Va. Code 55.1-1245; source)
  • Remediable breach: notice that agreement terminates not less than 30 days after receipt if not remedied in 21 days. (Va. Code 55.1-1245; source)
  • Non-remediable breach: termination not less than 30 days after notice. (Va. Code 55.1-1245; source)
  • If a dwelling is foreclosed and a tenant is in occupancy, a successor acquiring for primary residence must give notice to vacate at least 90 days out. (Va. Code Title 55.1 Ch. 12 (VRLTA), foreclosure successor provision; source)
  • A successor acquiring for any other purpose takes subject to the rental agreement and tenant may occupy for the remaining lease term, subject to termination under 55.1-1245. (VRLTA (foreclosure successor provision); source)
  • Residential executory contracts (installment, lease-option, rent-to-own) are subject to the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. (Va. Code 55.1-3002; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

This guide covers what official sources say about Virginia transfer on death deeds.

What the official sources say

  • Virginia's Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act begins at 64.2-621. (Va. Code 64.2-621 et seq. (referenced in 58.1-811); source)
  • TOD deed must state the transfer occurs at transferor's death and be recorded before death in the circuit court land records where the property is located. (Va. Code 64.2-628; source)
  • A TOD deed is revocable even if it says otherwise. (Va. Code 64.2-625; source)
  • A TOD deed transfers property without covenant or warranty of title. (Va. Code 64.2-632; source)
  • No recordation tax for a TOD deed or its revocation when no consideration passes. (Va. Code 58.1-811; source)
  • Small asset affidavit: personal probate estate not exceeding $75,000 and at least 60 days since death. (Va. Code 64.2-601; source)
  • If a will devises real estate to be sold and no other person is named, the executor has power to sell and convey it. (Va. Code 64.2-521; source)
  • Fiduciary transfers in administering a decedent's estate are exempt from the residential property disclosure statement requirement. (Va. Code 55.1-702; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Virginia counties hold tax sales of delinquent property.

What the official sources say

  • Real estate with taxes delinquent on December 31 after the second anniversary of the due date may be sold (first anniversary for condemned, nuisance, derelict, or blighted property). (Va. Code 58.1-3965; source)
  • Property assessed at $100,000 or less may be sold on court finding of taxes delinquent after first anniversary. (Va. Code 58.1-3965; source)
  • Treasurer must send notice at least 30 days before judicial proceedings and publish a list of properties. (Va. Code 58.1-3965; source)
  • Owner may redeem any time before the sale by paying all taxes, penalties, attorney fees, interest and costs; partial payment does not suffice. (Va. Code 58.1-3965; source)
  • Treasurer may suspend sale under an installment agreement not exceeding 72 months. (Va. Code 58.1-3965; source)
  • Owner, heirs, devisees, successors and assigns may redeem before the judicial sale date by paying into court taxes, penalties, interest, costs and attorney fee. (Va. Code 58.1-3974; source)
  • Real estate taxes are a lien on the property prior to any other lien or encumbrance until paid. (Va. Code 58.1-3340; source)
  • A money judgment becomes a lien on real estate when recorded on the judgment lien docket. (Va. Code 8.01-458; source)
  • Anyone who paid taxes on the real estate has a lien for taxes paid plus 6 percent annual interest. (Va. Code 58.1-3974; source)
